decks.title: Alternating Current — Part 1: rms values, reactance and phasors
goals: Relate the peak and rms values of an alternating current and voltage
Describe the phase relations for AC through a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor using phasors

slides.heading: Alternating Current
slides.body_md: Part 1 — voltages and currents that reverse direction many times a second, and how resistors, coils and capacitors respond to them.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: AC supply, peak and rms values, resistor, inductor, capacitor, phasors

slides.narration: The socket in your home gives alternating current, which reverses fifty times each way every second. AC is used because its voltage is easy to change with transformers. In this part we see how to describe an alternating voltage with peak and rms values, and how a resistor, an inductor and a capacitor each respond to it, using rotating arrows called phasors.

slides.heading: Alternating voltage and current
slides.body_md: A sinusoidal supply gives $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ with $\omega = 2\pi f$. In India $f = 50$ Hz, so $\omega \approx 314$ rad s$^{-1}$. The current in a resistor $R$ is $i = \dfrac{V_0}{R}\sin\omega t = I_0\sin\omega t$.
bullets: The average of $\sin\omega t$ over a cycle is zero, so the average current is zero.
The average of $\sin^2\omega t$ is 1/2, so the average power is not zero.

visual.alt: Sinusoidal alternating voltage between plus and minus its peak value, with the rms level at 0.707 of the peak marked
visual.caption: The rms value is 0.707 of the peak for a sinusoidal supply.

slides.narration: An alternating voltage swings smoothly between a positive and a negative peak. For Indian mains the frequency is fifty hertz, so omega is about three hundred and fourteen radians per second. Over a full cycle the current averages to zero, because it flows equally in both directions. But the heating does not cancel: the average of sine squared is one half, so power is delivered all the time.

slides.heading: Peak and rms values
slides.body_md:
The **rms (root-mean-square)** value is the steady (DC) value that would give the same average heating in a resistor:
$$\bar P = I_\text{rms}^2 R = \dfrac{I_0^2 R}{2}\ \Rightarrow\ I_\text{rms} = \dfrac{I_0}{\sqrt2} \approx 0.707I_0,\qquad V_\text{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2}$$
bullets: Mains voltage “220 V” is an rms value; the peak is about 311 V.
Ammeters and voltmeters for AC read rms values.

visual.alt: Sinusoidal alternating voltage between plus and minus its peak value, with the rms level at 0.707 of the peak marked
visual.caption: The rms value is 0.707 of the peak for a sinusoidal supply.

slides.narration: Because AC keeps changing, we quote an effective value. The rms value is the steady current that would heat a resistor at the same average rate. Average power is I nought squared R over two, so the rms current is the peak divided by root two, about seventy one percent of the peak. The two hundred and twenty volts of Indian mains is an rms value; the voltage actually peaks at about three hundred and eleven volts.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a heater on the mains
slides.body_md: A 1000 W heater runs on 220 V (rms), 50 Hz mains. Find the peak voltage, the rms current and the peak current.
bullets: Step 1 — $V_0 = \sqrt2 \times 220 \approx 311$ V.
Step 2 — $I_\text{rms} = \dfrac{P}{V_\text{rms}} = \dfrac{1000}{220} \approx 4.55$ A.
Step 3 — $I_0 = \sqrt2 \times 4.55 \approx 6.43$ A.

visual.alt: Worked table: 220 volts rms and 311 volts peak; 4.55 amperes rms and 6.43 amperes peak

slides.narration: Multiply the rms voltage by root two to get the peak, about three hundred and eleven volts. The power rating uses rms values, so the rms current is one thousand watts divided by two hundred and twenty volts, about four and a half amperes. The current peaks at about six point four amperes. Fuses and wiring must cope with these peaks.

slides.heading: Phasors
slides.body_md: A **phasor** is an arrow rotating anticlockwise at angular speed ω; its projection on the vertical axis gives the instantaneous value. The angle between two phasors is their **phase difference**.

slides.narration: Phasors make phase relations easy to see. Picture each sinusoidal quantity as an arrow of length equal to its peak, spinning anticlockwise at omega. The vertical projection is the instantaneous value. Arrows that point the same way are in phase; an arrow ahead in the anticlockwise sense leads, and one behind lags. The diagram shows the three basic cases.

slides.heading: AC through a pure inductor
slides.body_md:
For $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ across an inductor $L$: $L\dfrac{di}{dt} = v$ gives $i = I_0\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, with
$$I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{X_L},\qquad X_L = \omega L = 2\pi fL$$
The current **lags** the voltage by $\pi/2$. $X_L$ (ohm) is the **inductive reactance**.
bullets: $X_L$ grows with frequency: an inductor blocks high frequencies and passes DC freely.
Average power over a cycle is zero.

visual.alt: Voltage and current for a pure inductor: the current reaches each peak a quarter cycle after the voltage

slides.narration: For a pure inductor, the voltage equals L times the rate of change of current. Solving, the current is a sine wave lagging the voltage by a quarter cycle: it peaks a quarter period later. The peak current is the peak voltage divided by omega L, the inductive reactance, measured in ohms. The higher the frequency, the larger the reactance, so a coil lets steady current through but chokes rapid changes.

slides.heading: AC through a pure capacitor
slides.body_md:
For $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ across a capacitor $C$: $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = C\dfrac{dv}{dt}$ gives $i = I_0\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$, with
$$I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{X_C},\qquad X_C = \dfrac{1}{\omega C} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC}$$
The current **leads** the voltage by $\pi/2$. $X_C$ is the **capacitive reactance**.
bullets: $X_C$ falls with frequency: a capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies.
Average power over a cycle is zero.

slides.narration: A capacitor charges and discharges as the voltage alternates. The current is C times the rate of change of voltage, which makes it lead the voltage by a quarter cycle: the current is largest when the voltage is passing through zero. The peak current is the peak voltage divided by the capacitive reactance, one over omega C. At high frequency the reactance is small, so a capacitor passes rapid changes but blocks steady DC completely.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: reactances on the mains
slides.body_md: Find the reactance and the rms current when (a) a 0.50 H inductor, (b) a 20 μF capacitor is connected to 220 V, 50 Hz mains (resistance negligible).
bullets: (a) $X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.50 \approx 157$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{220}{157} \approx 1.40$ A, lagging by 90°.
(b) $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 20 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 159$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{220}{159} \approx 1.38$ A, leading by 90°.
Check — doubling f would double $X_L$ but halve $X_C$.

visual.alt: Worked table: 157 ohms and 1.40 amperes lagging for the inductor; 159 ohms and 1.38 amperes leading for the capacitor

slides.narration: At fifty hertz, omega is about three hundred and fourteen. The inductor’s reactance is omega L, about one hundred and fifty seven ohms, so about one point four amperes flows, lagging the voltage. The capacitor’s reactance is one over omega C, about one hundred and fifty nine ohms, so a similar current flows but leading the voltage. Doubling the frequency would double one reactance and halve the other.

slides.narration: Inductive reactance is omega L and capacitive reactance is one over omega C. See how each depends on frequency.

slides.heading: Comparing R, L and C in AC
slides.body_md: Summary of the three basic elements:
columns:
**Resistor**
- Opposition: R (any f)
- I in phase with V
- Average power $I_\text{rms}^2R$

**Inductor**
- Opposition: $X_L = \omega L$
- I lags V by 90°
- Average power 0

**Capacitor**
- Opposition: $X_C = 1/\omega C$
- I leads V by 90°
- Average power 0

**DC (f = 0)**
- Inductor: $X_L = 0$ (short)
- Capacitor: $X_C = \infty$ (open)

slides.narration: Here are the three elements side by side. A resistor opposes current equally at all frequencies, keeps current in phase, and absorbs power. An inductor’s opposition grows with frequency and its current lags; a capacitor’s opposition falls with frequency and its current leads. Neither of these two absorbs any average power. For steady DC, an ideal inductor is a plain wire and a capacitor is a gap.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: identifying a component
slides.body_md: A sealed box connected to a 50 Hz supply draws a current that leads the voltage by 90°. When the frequency is doubled, keeping the voltage the same, the current doubles. What is in the box?
bullets: Step 1 — current leading by 90° means a **pure capacitor** (no resistance).
Step 2 — check: $I = V/X_C = V\omega C$ is proportional to frequency, so doubling f doubles I. ✓
An inductor would have given a lagging current that halves when f doubles.

slides.heading: Summary — Part 1
slides.body_md: Key results:

rows: Power in pure L or C

visual.alt: Summary table of rms values and the behaviour of resistors, inductors and capacitors in AC

slides.narration: To sum up: the rms value of a sinusoidal current or voltage is the peak divided by root two, and it is the value meters read and appliances are rated in. In a resistor the current is in phase with the voltage. In an inductor it lags by a quarter cycle and the reactance is omega L. In a capacitor it leads by a quarter cycle and the reactance is one over omega C. Pure L and C take no average power.

slides.heading: Exam tips — Part 1
bullets: Mains values are rms: 220 V rms means about 311 V peak.
Remember **CIVIL**: in a C, I leads V; in an L, V leads I.
Use $\omega = 2\pi f$, not f, in reactances.
Derivations: write $v = V_0\sin\omega t$, use $L\,di/dt = v$ or $i = C\,dv/dt$, then read off the phase.

visual.alt: Table of how inductive and capacitive reactance change when the frequency is doubled or reduced to zero

slides.narration: Remember that mains figures are rms values. A memory aid for phase is CIVIL: in a capacitor, current leads voltage; in an inductor, voltage leads current. Always use omega, two pi f, in the reactance formulas. And in derivations, start from the voltage as a sine function and differentiate or integrate to find the current and its phase.

slides.heading: LCR circuits, power and transformers
slides.body_md: Part 2 — combining R, L and C in series, resonance, the power actually used in AC circuits, and the machines that make and transform AC.

visual.alt: Flow of the part: series LCR, impedance, resonance, power factor, generator, transformer

slides.narration: Real circuits combine resistance, inductance and capacitance. In this part we use phasors to find the total opposition, the impedance, and see how a radio tunes in one station by resonance. Then we find the real power used in AC circuits and why power companies care about power factor. Finally we look at the generator that produces AC and the transformer that changes its voltage.

slides.heading: Series LCR circuit: phasor diagram
slides.body_md:
The same current $I$ flows through all three. Take $I$ as reference: $V_R = IR$ in phase, $V_L = IX_L$ ahead by 90°, $V_C = IX_C$ behind by 90°. Adding the phasors:
$$V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2} = I\sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$$

slides.narration: In a series circuit the current is common, so draw it as the reference. The resistor’s voltage is in phase with it, the inductor’s voltage points ninety degrees ahead, and the capacitor’s ninety degrees behind. The inductor and capacitor voltages point in opposite directions, so they partly cancel. The supply voltage is the phasor sum: the square root of V R squared plus V L minus V C squared.

slides.heading: Impedance and phase angle
slides.body_md:
$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\qquad I = \dfrac{V}{Z},\qquad \tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$
$\phi$ is the angle by which the voltage leads the current.
bullets: $X_L > X_C$: inductive circuit, V leads I.
$X_C > X_L$: capacitive circuit, I leads V.
$X_L = X_C$: resistive, in phase (resonance).

slides.narration: The total opposition of a series LCR circuit is the impedance Z, the square root of R squared plus X L minus X C squared, which forms the impedance triangle. The current is the voltage divided by Z. The phase angle phi, from tan phi equals X L minus X C over R, tells you whether the circuit behaves inductively, with voltage leading, or capacitively, with current leading.

slides.body_md: A series circuit has $R = 30$ Ω, $X_L = 80$ Ω and $X_C = 40$ Ω, connected to 220 V rms. Find Z, the current, the voltage across each element and the phase angle.
bullets: Step 3 — $\tan\phi = \dfrac{40}{30}$, so $\phi \approx 53.1^\circ$; voltage leads current (inductive).
Note — $V_L$ alone (352 V) exceeds the supply voltage: phasors, not plain numbers, must add up to 220 V.

slides.narration: The net reactance is forty ohms, so with thirty ohms of resistance the impedance is fifty ohms, a three four five triangle, and the current is four point four amperes. The voltages across the parts are one hundred and thirty two, three hundred and fifty two and one hundred and seventy six volts. They add as phasors, not as numbers, to two hundred and twenty volts. The voltage leads by about fifty three degrees.

slides.heading: Resonance
slides.body_md:
The current is largest when $X_L = X_C$, i.e. $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$:
$$\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}},\qquad f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$
At resonance $Z = R$ (minimum), $I = V/R$ (maximum), and V and I are in phase.
bullets: Smaller R gives a sharper, taller peak: better selection of one frequency.
Radio tuning: the capacitor is varied until $f_0$ matches the station.

visual.alt: Current against angular frequency for a series LCR circuit: a peak at the resonant frequency, sharp and tall when the resistance is small, broad and low when it is larger
visual.caption: Peak height V/R; sharpness increases as R decreases.

slides.narration: As the frequency of the supply changes, X L rises and X C falls. At one frequency they are equal and cancel, leaving only the resistance. This is resonance, at omega nought equal to one over root L C. The current is then as large as it can be and in phase with the voltage. A small resistance gives a tall, sharp peak, which is how a radio picks out one station from many.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: resonant frequency
slides.body_md: A series circuit has $L = 0.10$ H, $C = 10\,\mu\text{F}$ and $R = 20$ Ω, with a 100 V rms variable-frequency supply. Find the resonant angular frequency, the resonant frequency and the current at resonance.
bullets: Step 1 — $\omega_0 = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{0.10 \times 10 \times 10^{-6}}} = 1000$ rad s$^{-1}$.
Step 2 — $f_0 = \dfrac{\omega_0}{2\pi} \approx 159$ Hz.
Step 3 — at resonance $Z = R$: $I = \dfrac{100}{20} = 5$ A.

visual.alt: Current against angular frequency for a series LCR circuit: a peak at the resonant frequency, sharp and tall when the resistance is small, broad and low when it is larger
visual.caption: Peak height V/R; sharpness increases as R decreases.

slides.narration: Multiply L and C to get ten to the minus six, take the square root and invert: omega nought is one thousand radians per second. Divide by two pi for the frequency, about one hundred and fifty nine hertz. At resonance the reactances cancel, so only the twenty ohm resistance limits the current: five amperes, the largest the circuit can draw from this supply.

slides.body_md: Choose the correct statement about a series LCR circuit at resonance.

slides.narration: At resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances are equal. What does that leave for the impedance and the phase?

slides.heading: Power in AC circuits
slides.body_md:
The average power is
$$P = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$$
$\cos\phi$ is the **power factor** ($= R/Z$ for series LCR).
bullets: Pure R: $\cos\phi = 1$, $P = VI$.
Pure L or C: $\phi = 90^\circ$, $P = 0$.
Only the resistance dissipates power: $P = I_\text{rms}^2R$.

slides.narration: In AC the current and voltage may be out of step, so the average power is not simply V times I. It is V rms times I rms times cos phi, and cos phi is called the power factor. For a pure resistor it is one. For a pure inductor or capacitor the phase is ninety degrees, the power factor is zero, and no average power is used: energy is stored and returned each cycle. Only resistance dissipates power.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: power factor
slides.body_md: Find the power factor and the average power for the circuit of worked example 4 ($R = 30$ Ω, $Z = 50$ Ω, $I = 4.4$ A, 220 V).
bullets: Step 1 — $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{30}{50} = 0.60$.
Step 2 — $P = VI\cos\phi = 220 \times 4.4 \times 0.6 = 580.8$ W.
Check — $I^2R = 4.4^2 \times 30 = 580.8$ W: the same, since only R dissipates power.

slides.narration: The power factor is R over Z, thirty over fifty, zero point six. The apparent power, volts times amperes, is about nine hundred and sixty eight, but only sixty percent of it is real power: about five hundred and eighty one watts. Check with I squared R: four point four squared times thirty gives the same figure, because the coil and capacitor return all the energy they take.

slides.heading: Power factor and wattless current
slides.body_md: The current can be split into a part **in phase** with V, $I\cos\phi$, which delivers power, and a part **90° out of phase**, $I\sin\phi$, which delivers none: the **wattless current**.
bullets: A low power factor means a large current for little power, so large $I^2R$ losses in supply lines.
Industries add capacitors to cancel the inductive reactance of motors and raise the power factor towards 1.

visual.alt: Table of power factors of typical loads: heaters near one, lightly loaded motors 0.3 to 0.5, motors with correcting capacitors 0.9 to 1

slides.narration: Think of the current as two parts. The part in step with the voltage, I cos phi, carries the real power. The part a quarter cycle out of step, I sin phi, flows back and forth without delivering any average power, so it is called wattless current. It still heats the supply cables, so a low power factor wastes energy. Factories with big motors add capacitors to improve their power factor.

slides.heading: Quick check: wattless current
slides.body_md: Decide whether the statement is true or false.
slides.narration: Ask whether a current exactly a quarter cycle out of phase with the voltage delivers any average power.

slides.heading: The AC generator
slides.body_md:
A coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotates with angular speed $\omega$ in a uniform field $B$. The flux is $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, so
$$\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t,\qquad \varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$$
bullets: Slip rings and brushes connect the rotating coil to the external circuit.
The emf is largest when the plane of the coil is parallel to B (flux changing fastest).

By Faraday’s law the emf is N B A omega sine omega t, an alternating emf with peak N B A omega. It is largest when the coil’s plane lies along the field, where the flux is zero but changing fastest. Slip rings and brushes carry the current out.

slides.heading: The transformer
slides.body_md:
Two coils on a common laminated iron core. An alternating current in the primary makes an alternating flux that links the secondary. For an **ideal** transformer:
$$\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$$
bullets: Step-up: $N_s > N_p$; step-down: $N_s < N_p$.
Ideal: power in = power out, $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$.
Losses: copper ($I^2R$) in windings, flux leakage, hysteresis and core heating (reduced by laminating the core).
Works only with AC: a steady current gives no changing flux.

slides.narration: A transformer has two coils wound on one iron core. Alternating current in the primary creates an alternating flux in the core, which induces an emf in the secondary. Each turn gets the same emf, so the voltages are in the ratio of the turns. If no energy is lost, power in equals power out, so stepping the voltage up steps the current down. Laminating the core reduces energy losses, and a transformer cannot work with steady DC.

slides.heading: Worked example 8: a step-down transformer
slides.body_md: An ideal transformer has a turns ratio $N_p : N_s = 20 : 1$ and is connected to 220 V mains. The secondary supplies 2.0 A. Find the secondary voltage and the primary current.
bullets: Step 1 — $V_s = V_p\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{220}{20} = 11$ V.
Step 2 — power conservation: $I_p = I_s\dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{2.0}{20} = 0.10$ A.
Check — power in $220 \times 0.10 = 22$ W equals power out $11 \times 2.0 = 22$ W.

slides.narration: To sum up: in a series LCR circuit the voltages add as phasors, giving the impedance root R squared plus X L minus X C squared and a phase angle with tan phi equal to the net reactance over R. A generator gives N B A omega sine omega t, and a transformer changes voltage in the ratio of the turns.

notes.title: Alternating Current — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Peak and rms values
sections.body_md:
A sinusoidal supply: $v = V_0\sin\omega t$, $\omega = 2\pi f$ (India: 50 Hz, ω ≈ 314 rad s⁻¹). The average current over a cycle is zero, but the average of $\sin^2$ is 1/2, so power is delivered.

**rms value:** the steady value giving the same average heating: $\bar P = I_\text{rms}^2R = \tfrac12 I_0^2R$, so $I_\text{rms} = I_0/\sqrt2 \approx 0.707I_0$ and $V_\text{rms} = V_0/\sqrt2$. AC meters read rms; “220 V mains” is rms (peak ≈ 311 V).

key_terms.definition_md: The steady (DC) value that produces the same average heating in a resistor; I₀/√2 for a sinusoid.

visual.alt: Sinusoidal alternating voltage between plus and minus its peak value, with the rms level at 0.707 of the peak marked
visual.caption: The rms value is 0.707 of the peak for a sinusoidal supply.

sections.heading: 2. AC through R, L and C; reactance
sections.body_md:
| Element | Opposition | Phase of I relative to V | Average power |
|---|---|---|---|
| R | R | in phase | $I_\text{rms}^2R$ |
| L | $X_L = \omega L$ | lags by π/2 | 0 |
| C | $X_C = 1/\omega C$ | leads by π/2 | 0 |

- Inductor: $L\,di/dt = V_0\sin\omega t$ gives $i = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}\sin(\omega t - \pi/2)$.
- Capacitor: $i = C\,dv/dt = \omega CV_0\cos\omega t = \dfrac{V_0}{1/\omega C}\sin(\omega t + \pi/2)$.
- $X_L \propto f$ (blocks high frequencies, passes DC); $X_C \propto 1/f$ (blocks DC, passes high frequencies).
- **Phasors:** arrows of length equal to the peak value rotating anticlockwise at ω; projections give instantaneous values; angles give phase differences.

key_terms.definition_md: X_L = ωL, the opposition of an inductor to AC.
X_C = 1/ωC, the opposition of a capacitor to AC.

sections.heading: 3. Series LCR circuit and resonance
sections.body_md:
Same current through all; voltages add as phasors: $V = \sqrt{V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2}$.

$$Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2},\qquad I = V/Z,\qquad \tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$$
$X_L > X_C$: inductive (V leads I); $X_C > X_L$: capacitive (I leads V).

**Resonance:** $X_L = X_C$ at $\omega_0 = 1/\sqrt{LC}$, $f_0 = 1/2\pi\sqrt{LC}$. Then $Z = R$ (minimum), $I = V/R$ (maximum), φ = 0. Smaller R gives a sharper resonance — used in radio tuning. Voltages across L and C at resonance can be much larger than the supply voltage.

key_terms.definition_md: Total opposition of an AC circuit, Z = V/I.
Condition X_L = X_C at which a series LCR circuit carries maximum current.

sections.heading: 4. Power, power factor and wattless current
sections.body_md:
Average power $P = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$; **power factor** $\cos\phi = R/Z$ (series LCR).

- Pure R: cos φ = 1. Pure L or C: cos φ = 0 (energy stored and returned each cycle). At resonance: 1.
- Only resistance dissipates: $P = I_\text{rms}^2R$.
- **Wattless current:** the component $I\sin\phi$, 90° out of phase with V, delivers no average power but still causes $I^2R$ loss in the supply lines. Capacitors are added to inductive loads (motors) to raise the power factor.

key_terms.definition_md: cos φ, the ratio of real power to the product V_rms I_rms.
The component of current 90° out of phase with the voltage; it consumes no average power.

sections.heading: 5. AC generator and transformer
sections.body_md:
**AC generator:** a coil (N turns, area A) rotates at ω in field B: $\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$, $\varepsilon = NBA\omega\sin\omega t$, peak $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$ (largest when the coil’s plane is parallel to B). Slip rings and brushes connect the coil to the circuit. Mechanical energy → electrical energy.

**Transformer:** primary and secondary on a laminated soft-iron core; works by mutual induction, AC only.
- Ideal: $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p} = \dfrac{I_p}{I_s}$; power in = power out.
- Step-up ($N_s > N_p$) for transmission; step-down for distribution and chargers.
- Losses: copper ($I^2R$, thick wires), flux leakage (interleaved windings), hysteresis (soft iron), heating of the core by induced currents (laminated core).

key_terms.definition_md: A device that changes an alternating voltage using mutual induction between two coils on a common core.
N_s/N_p, equal to V_s/V_p for an ideal transformer.

questions.stem_md: An alternating voltage has a peak value of 311 V. Find its rms value, in volts (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $V_\text{rms} = \dfrac{V_0}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{311}{1.414} \approx 220$ V.

questions.solution_md: Meters read rms, so $I_0 = \sqrt2 \times 5.0 \approx 7.07$ A — option (a).

A lamp is rated 60 W, 220 V for AC mains. The peak current through it is about

questions.stem_md: True or false? Because the average value of an alternating current over a cycle is zero, a heater connected to AC mains produces no heat.
questions.solution_md: False. The heating depends on i², whose average over a cycle is I₀²/2, not zero. That is why rms values are used.

questions.stem_md: What is meant by the rms value of an alternating current? Why is it used instead of the average value?

answer.model_answer_md: The **rms value** is the steady (DC) current that would produce the **same average heating** in a resistor as the alternating current; for a sinusoid it is $I_0/\sqrt2$. The **average** value over a full cycle is **zero**, which says nothing about the heating effect, so rms values are used for ratings and meters.

questions.solution_md: Define by equal heating; average is zero.

questions.solution_md: $X_L = \omega L \propto f$ and $X_C = 1/\omega C \propto 1/f$ — option (b).

**Assertion (A):** In a circuit containing only a capacitor, the current leads the voltage by 90°.

**Reason (R):** The charging current is largest when the voltage is changing fastest, which is when the voltage passes through zero.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution_md: Both true; since $i = C\,dv/dt$, the current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage does, which is exactly what R describes — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Find the reactance of a 0.20 H inductor at 50 Hz, in ohms (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $X_L = 2\pi fL = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.20 \approx 62.8$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: Find the reactance of a 50 μF capacitor at 50 Hz, in ohms (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi fC} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 63.7$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: At what frequency does a 0.10 H inductor have a reactance of 314 Ω? Answer in hertz (3 significant figures).
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{X_L}{2\pi L} = \dfrac{314}{2\pi \times 0.10} \approx 500$ Hz.

questions.stem_md: At what frequency does a 1.0 H inductor have the same reactance as a 1.0 μF capacitor?
questions.solution_md: $\omega L = \dfrac{1}{\omega C}$ gives $\omega = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{LC}} = 1000$ rad s$^{-1}$, so $f = \dfrac{1000}{2\pi} \approx 159$ Hz — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each element connected alone to an AC supply (Column A) with its property (Column B).
questions.solution_md: Resistor → in phase (1 → s); inductor → X ∝ f (2 → p); capacitor → blocks DC (3 → r); resonance → Z = R (4 → q).

questions.stem_md: Explain why a capacitor blocks a steady (DC) current but allows an alternating current to flow in the circuit.

answer.model_answer_md: With DC the capacitor simply **charges up** and then no more charge flows: $X_C = 1/\omega C$ is **infinite** at ω = 0. With AC the voltage keeps **reversing**, so the capacitor keeps **charging and discharging**, and charge flows back and forth in the wires; $X_C$ is finite and falls as the frequency rises.

questions.solution_md: X_C infinite at f = 0, finite for AC.

marking_scheme.step: DC: charges once, then no current (X_C infinite)

questions.stem_md: Two identical lamps are connected to the same variable-frequency AC supply, one in series with an inductor and the other in series with a capacitor. Predict what happens to each lamp as the frequency is raised, and explain.

answer.model_answer_md: The lamp with the **inductor** becomes **dimmer**, because $X_L = \omega L$ rises with frequency. The lamp with the **capacitor** becomes **brighter**, because $X_C = 1/\omega C$ falls with frequency. (At one frequency the two lamps are equally bright, when $X_L = X_C$.)

questions.solution_md: X_L rises, X_C falls with frequency.

questions.stem_md: A voltage $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ is applied across a pure inductor $L$. Derive the current, and show that it lags the voltage by π/2. Write the inductive reactance.

answer.model_answer_md: The induced emf balances the applied voltage: $L\dfrac{di}{dt} = V_0\sin\omega t$. Integrating, $i = -\dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}\cos\omega t = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}\sin\left(\omega t - \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. So $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \pi/2)$ with $I_0 = \dfrac{V_0}{\omega L}$: the current **lags** the voltage by π/2. The inductive reactance is $X_L = \omega L$.

The impedance is zero and the current is infinite
The current lags the voltage by 90°
The voltages across L and C are both zero

questions.stem_md: A series circuit has R = 8.0 Ω, L = 50 mH and C = 100 μF, connected to a 100 V rms, 50 Hz supply. Find the reactances, the impedance and the rms current, and state whether the current leads or lags.

answer.model_answer_md:
$X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.050 \approx 15.7$ Ω; $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 100 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 31.8$ Ω.

questions.stem_md: Why is a choke coil (an inductor of very low resistance) used, instead of a resistor, to reduce the current in an AC circuit?

Because its resistance is very small, the phase difference is close to **90°**, so the power it consumes, $VI\cos\phi$, is nearly **zero**. A resistor would limit the current too, but would waste energy as **heat** ($I^2R$).

questions.stem_md: Explain what is meant by wattless current, using a phasor diagram. A circuit draws 10 A rms with the current lagging the voltage by 60°. Find the power (active) component and the wattless component of the current.

answer.model_answer_md:
Resolve the current phasor into a component **along** the voltage, $I\cos\phi$, and one **perpendicular** to it, $I\sin\phi$. Only $I\cos\phi$ contributes to the average power $VI\cos\phi$; the perpendicular component carries no average power and is the **wattless current**.
Active component $= 10\cos 60^\circ = 5.0$ A; wattless component $= 10\sin 60^\circ \approx 8.66$ A.

options.text_md: the emf is the same at all instants

questions.stem_md: The speed of rotation of an AC generator’s coil is doubled. The peak emf and the frequency of the output become
questions.solution_md: ε₀ = NBAω is proportional to ω, and the output frequency equals the rotation frequency — option (c).

options.text_md: reduce energy lost as heat by currents induced in the core

allow the transformer to work on DC

questions.stem_md: Why is electric power transmitted over long distances at very high voltages, using step-up and step-down transformers?

answer.model_answer_md: For a given power $P = VI$, a **higher voltage** means a **smaller current**. Line losses are $I^2R$, so they fall in proportion to $1/V^2$. Transformers step the voltage **up** at the power station for transmission and **down** near the consumer for safe use; they work efficiently only with AC.

questions.solution_md: P = VI fixed; loss I²R.

marking_scheme.step: Higher V, smaller I for same power
Smaller I²R loss; transformers step up and down

questions.stem_md: State three sources of energy loss in a real transformer and how each is reduced.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) **Copper loss:** $I^2R$ heating in the windings — use thick copper wire. (2) **Core heating by induced currents** — use a laminated core of thin insulated sheets. (3) **Hysteresis loss** in repeatedly magnetising the core — use soft iron, which magnetises and demagnetises easily. (Also **flux leakage**, reduced by winding the coils one over the other.)

questions.solution_md: Copper, core currents, hysteresis, leakage.

questions.stem_md: (a) A voltage $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ is applied across a capacitor $C$. Derive the current and show that it leads the voltage by π/2. (b) Show on a graph or phasor diagram how $v$ and $i$ vary, and explain why the average power is zero. (c) A 25 μF capacitor is connected to 220 V, 50 Hz mains. Find its reactance and the rms current.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The charge is $q = Cv = CV_0\sin\omega t$, so $i = \dfrac{dq}{dt} = \omega CV_0\cos\omega t = \dfrac{V_0}{1/\omega C}\sin\left(\omega t + \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$. Thus $I_0 = V_0/X_C$ with $X_C = 1/\omega C$, and the current **leads** the voltage by π/2.

(b) On the phasor diagram the current phasor is 90° ahead (anticlockwise) of the voltage phasor; on a graph the current peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage. The power $vi \propto \sin\omega t\cos\omega t = \tfrac12\sin 2\omega t$ is positive for one quarter cycle (charging) and negative for the next (energy returned), so its average is **zero**.

(c) $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 25 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 127$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{220}{127} \approx 1.73$ A.

questions.solution_md: i = C dv/dt; average of sin 2ωt is zero.

marking_scheme.step: i = C dv/dt and the phase lead π/2
Phasor/graph and zero average power explained

questions.stem_md: (a) Draw (describe) the phasor diagram of a series LCR circuit and derive its impedance and phase angle. (b) A series circuit has R = 60 Ω, L = 0.40 H and C = 50 μF, connected to 220 V, 50 Hz. Find the impedance, the current and the phase angle. (c) Find the frequency at which the current would be largest, and that current.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) The current $I$ is common, so take it as reference. $V_R = IR$ is along $I$; $V_L = IX_L$ is 90° ahead; $V_C = IX_C$ is 90° behind. Adding: $V^2 = V_R^2 + (V_L - V_C)^2 = I^2[R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2]$, so $Z = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}$ and $\tan\phi = \dfrac{X_L - X_C}{R}$ (voltage leads by φ if positive).

(b) $X_L = 2\pi \times 50 \times 0.40 \approx 126$ Ω; $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 63.7$ Ω. $Z = \sqrt{60^2 + (126 - 63.7)^2} \approx 86.3$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{220}{86.3} \approx 2.55$ A; $\tan\phi = \dfrac{62.0}{60}$, $\phi \approx 45.9^\circ$ (voltage leads; inductive).

(c) Resonance: $f_0 = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}} = \dfrac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{0.40 \times 50 \times 10^{-6}}} \approx 35.6$ Hz; then $Z = R$ and $I = \dfrac{220}{60} \approx 3.67$ A.

questions.solution_md: Phasor sum with I as reference; then numbers; then resonance.

marking_scheme.step: Phasor diagram and Z, tan φ derived

questions.stem_md: (a) Show that the average power in an AC circuit is $V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$. (b) Explain the terms power factor and wattless current, and why a low power factor is undesirable. (c) A coil of resistance 40 Ω and reactance 30 Ω is connected to a 230 V rms supply. Find the current, the power factor and the average power.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) With $v = V_0\sin\omega t$ and $i = I_0\sin(\omega t - \phi)$, the instantaneous power is $vi = V_0I_0\sin\omega t\sin(\omega t - \phi) = \tfrac12 V_0I_0[\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t - \phi)]$. The second term averages to zero over a cycle, so $\bar P = \tfrac12 V_0I_0\cos\phi = V_\text{rms}I_\text{rms}\cos\phi$.

(b) **Power factor** is $\cos\phi$. **Wattless current** is the component $I\sin\phi$ perpendicular to the voltage, which carries no average power. A low power factor means a large current for the power delivered, so larger $I^2R$ losses in cables and generators.

(c) $Z = \sqrt{40^2 + 30^2} = 50$ Ω; $I = \dfrac{230}{50} = 4.6$ A; $\cos\phi = \dfrac{40}{50} = 0.8$; $P = I^2R = 4.6^2 \times 40 \approx 846$ W (also $230 \times 4.6 \times 0.8 \approx 846$ W).

questions.solution_md: Average the product of v and i; then Z, I, cos φ, P.

marking_scheme.step: Power factor and wattless current explained

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain the principle and working of an AC generator. (b) Derive the expression for the emf induced in its rotating coil. (c) A coil of 500 turns, each of area 0.030 m², rotates at 3000 revolutions per minute in a field of 0.20 T. Find the peak and rms emf and the frequency of the output.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Principle:** electromagnetic induction — a coil rotating in a magnetic field has a continuously changing flux, so an alternating emf is induced. **Working:** an armature coil is turned (by a turbine) between the poles of a magnet; its ends are connected to **slip rings**, which turn with it and press against fixed carbon **brushes** that lead the current to the external circuit.

(b) If the normal to the coil makes angle $\theta = \omega t$ with $\vec B$, the flux linkage is $N\Phi = NBA\cos\omega t$. So $\varepsilon = -\dfrac{d(N\Phi)}{dt} = NBA\omega\sin\omega t = \varepsilon_0\sin\omega t$, with $\varepsilon_0 = NBA\omega$.

(c) $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi \times 3000}{60} \approx 314$ rad s$^{-1}$; $\varepsilon_0 = 500 \times 0.20 \times 0.030 \times 314 \approx 942$ V; $\varepsilon_\text{rms} \approx 666$ V; frequency 50 Hz.

questions.solution_md: Flux NBA cos ωt; differentiate.

questions.stem_md: (a) Explain the principle and working of a transformer and derive $V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p$ for an ideal transformer. (b) A transformer steps 11 000 V down to 220 V and delivers 33 kW to houses. Find the turns ratio and the secondary current. (c) If its efficiency is 90%, find the input power and the primary current.

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Principle:** mutual induction. An alternating current in the primary produces an alternating flux $\Phi$ in the soft-iron core, which links every turn of both coils. The emfs are $\varepsilon_p = -N_p\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$ and $\varepsilon_s = -N_s\dfrac{d\Phi}{dt}$. For an ideal transformer (no resistance, no flux leakage) $V_p = \varepsilon_p$ and $V_s = \varepsilon_s$, so $\dfrac{V_s}{V_p} = \dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$; with no losses $V_pI_p = V_sI_s$.

(b) $\dfrac{N_p}{N_s} = \dfrac{11\,000}{220} = 50$, i.e. 50 : 1. $I_s = \dfrac{33\,000}{220} = 150$ A.

(c) Input power $= \dfrac{33\,000}{0.90} \approx 36700$ W; $I_p = \dfrac{36\,700}{11\,000} \approx 3.33$ A.

questions.solution_md: Same dΦ/dt per turn in both coils; then ratios and efficiency.

questions.passage_md: Older ceiling-fan regulators in Indian homes used a resistor in series with the fan to reduce its speed; they got warm and wasted energy. Modern “electronic” step regulators often use a capacitor in series with the fan instead. On one speed setting, a 2.25 μF capacitor is used on 220 V, 50 Hz mains.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (d) An ideal capacitor takes no average power, because its current is 90° out of phase with its voltage

**(b)** 1410 Ω

**(c)** (i) A **smaller** capacitor. Its reactance $X_C = 1/\omega C$ is **larger**, so it limits the current through the fan more and the fan runs **slower**. A larger capacitor has a smaller reactance and lets the fan run faster.

**OR** (ii) The resistor’s current is **in phase** with its voltage, so it dissipates $I^2R$ continuously as **heat**. In the capacitor the current is **90° out of phase**, so the average power is **zero**: it stores and returns energy each cycle and does not heat up (apart from small losses).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** For a pure capacitor cos φ = 0: energy stored in one quarter cycle is returned in the next — option (d).

**(b)** $X_C = \dfrac{1}{2\pi \times 50 \times 2.25 \times 10^{-6}} \approx 1410$ Ω.

**(c)** (i) X_C ∝ 1/C.

(ii) Compare cos φ = 1 and cos φ = 0.

children.stem_md: Why does the capacitor regulator waste almost no energy?

options.text_md: A capacitor has zero reactance at 50 Hz
The capacitor stores all the energy permanently
A capacitor raises the mains voltage
An ideal capacitor takes no average power, because its current is 90° out of phase with its voltage

children.solution_md: For a pure capacitor cos φ = 0: energy stored in one quarter cycle is returned in the next — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** An ideal inductor offers a large opposition to a steady direct current.

**Reason (R):** The reactance of an inductor is ωL, which is proportional to frequency.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: R is true. A is false: for DC, ω = 0, so X_L = 0 and an ideal inductor offers no opposition — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a series LCR circuit, the rms voltages across R, L and C cannot be added arithmetically to give the supply voltage.

**Reason (R):** These voltages are not in phase with one another.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both true; because V_L and V_C are ±90° from V_R, they add as phasors, not as numbers — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The emf of an AC generator is zero when the plane of its coil is perpendicular to the magnetic field.

**Reason (R):** The flux through the coil is zero when its plane is perpendicular to the field.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: in that position the flux is MAXIMUM (but momentarily not changing), which is why the emf is zero — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A step-up transformer increases the voltage and also increases the power delivered.
questions.solution_md: False. An ideal transformer conserves power: if it steps the voltage up, it steps the current down by the same ratio; a real one delivers slightly less power than it takes.

questions.stem_md: A coil of negligible resistance draws 2.0 A from a 220 V, 50 Hz supply. What current will it draw from a 220 V, 100 Hz supply? Answer in amperes.
questions.solution_md: At 50 Hz, $X_L = \dfrac{220}{2.0} = 110$ Ω. Doubling the frequency doubles $X_L$ to 220 Ω, so $I = \dfrac{220}{220} = 1$ A.

questions.stem_md: A series LCR circuit with R = 5.0 Ω is connected to a 10 V rms supply whose frequency is adjusted to resonance. The rms current is
questions.solution_md: At resonance Z = R, so $I = \dfrac{10}{5.0} = 2$ A — option (b).

questions.stem_md: In a series LCR circuit at resonance, the capacitance is made four times larger. To restore resonance at the same frequency, the inductance must be
questions.solution_md: ω₀ = 1/√(LC) is unchanged only if LC is unchanged, so L must become L/4 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A series AC circuit has resistance 50 Ω and impedance 100 Ω. Find the phase angle between the voltage and the current, in degrees.
questions.solution_md: $\cos\phi = \dfrac{R}{Z} = \dfrac{50}{100} = 0.5$, so $\phi = 60$ degrees.

questions.stem_md: A transformer in a mains adaptor steps 220 V down to 5.0 V. Its secondary has 50 turns. How many turns does the primary have?
questions.solution_md: $N_p = N_s\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = 50 \times \dfrac{220}{5.0} = 2200$ turns.
